title: Yama comes himself
hook: Savitri walks into the forest beside Satyavan on the day itself, and Death comes for him in person
carry: the body dies; the self is not slain

segments.voice: Yesterday: vrata, Savitri's three-night vow, the root of a fast women still keep. Your line was a vrata is a vow kept with the body.

Satyavan shoulders his axe. He's heading into the woods for fruit and firewood, as he does every morning. And Savitri, who has eaten nothing through her vow, asks to come along. He's surprised. You've never come before, he says; the path is hard, and you're weak from fasting. She won't be talked out of it. She even asks his parents' leave, and they give it. So the two of them set off together, and the epic says she looks cheerful while her heart is burning.
screen: `AN AXE AND A FOREST PATH.` → `SHE ASKS TO COME ALONG.` → `CHEERFUL, WITH A BURNING HEART.`

segments.voice: Satyavan shows her the forest as they walk, the streams and the flowering trees. He gathers fruit and starts to split wood. Then he stops. His head aches, he says. He wants to lie down. Savitri sits on the ground and takes his head into her lap. And then she sees someone: a tall figure, dark, dressed in red, a noose in his hand, standing over Satyavan. She lays her husband's head down gently, stands, joins her palms and asks who he is. He is Yama, lord of death, and Satyavan's time has come. Why have you come yourself, she asks, and not your messengers? Because Satyavan was good, Yama answers, not someone to be fetched by servants. And with his noose he draws out of Satyavan's body a person no bigger than a thumb. Now the teaching in that detail. The Upanishads describe the self within each of us as a person the size of a thumb. What Yama takes is not the body; the body lies still on the ground. What leaves is the self, the one who lived in it. This is the Hindu view of death: the body dies, and the self is not slain. The Bhagavad Gita says it plainly: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves a worn-out body and takes another. And Yama is also called Dharmaraja, king of dharma: in this tradition, death keeps a just order. So Yama turns south with what he's taken. And Savitri does what no one does. She follows. For today: when someone dies, Hindus grieve, and also hold this: the one we loved was never only the body.
screen: `HIS HEAD IN HER LAP.` · `A DARK FIGURE WITH A NOOSE.` · `A PERSON THE SIZE OF A THUMB.` · `THE BODY DIES; THE SELF IS NOT SLAIN.` · then, large: `SAVITRI FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus, remembering someone who has died, say om shanti: peace. Bring to mind someone you've lost, and let one good memory of them come back. Then, if you pray, say om shanti softly three times for them; if not, simply wish them peace, wherever they are, and stay with the memory a while.
Yama. Lord of death, called Dharmaraja, king of dharma, who takes the self and leaves the body, and finds Savitri following.
Your line: the body dies; the self is not slain. And Savitri isn't done. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's telling, Yama comes for Satyavan in person and draws out a thumb-sized person with his noose, the self the Upanishads describe; the Bhagavad Gita teaches that the self is not slain when the body is.
